title: Policy Administration Systems (PAS) for Life Insurance

blocks.h: On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

items.h: Define a Policy Administration System (PAS) and explain its role as the central operational infrastructure of a life insurance company, distinguishing it from adjacent systems such as CRM, actuarial systems, and financial accounting platforms.

Describe the eight core functional modules of a life insurance PAS (new business processing, policy issuance, premium collection, policy maintenance, benefit calculation, claims processing, reinsurance cession, and financial reporting) and explain the data flows and dependencies between each module.

Explain the criteria for selecting a PAS for a Nigerian life insurer, covering scalability, regulatory compliance (NIIRA 2025 and IFRS 17), API-readiness, vendor support, total cost of ownership, and the specific Nigerian market requirements that international PAS vendors may not natively support.

Describe the key reports that a well-configured life insurance PAS must produce (the in-force register, lapse and conservation reports, new business summary, claims register, reinsurance cession statements, and premium reconciliation) and explain how each report is used in operational management and regulatory reporting.

Evaluate the merits and limitations of cloud-based versus on-premise PAS deployment for Nigerian life insurers, considering cost, security, regulatory compliance (NDPA 2023), scalability, and the specific constraints of the Nigerian technology infrastructure environment.

Describe the principal integration interfaces between a life insurance PAS and adjacent systems (core banking systems [for bancassurance], CRM platforms, actuarial modelling systems, regulatory reporting tools, and digital customer portals) and explain how API-based integration enables real-time data exchange across these systems.

Explain the specific NIIRA 2025 and NDPA 2023 compliance obligations that a life insurer’s PAS must satisfy, including audit trail requirements, data localisation, access controls, data subject rights support, and the actuarial data integrity requirements for IFRS 17 reporting.

Describe the major PAS vendors and platforms operating in the African and Nigerian market, explaining the key differentiators between global enterprise platforms, regional African solutions, and bespoke internally developed systems.

Explain the principal risks and failure modes of a PAS implementation project, and describe the governance framework, project management approach, and testing regime required to successfully implement or migrate a life insurance PAS.
Design a PAS assessment framework for a Nigerian life insurer evaluating its current system and determining whether to upgrade, replace, or augment it with complementary digital tools.

blocks.text: 29.1 Introduction: The PAS as the Insurer’s Operational Core

blocks.h: If a life insurance company is a machine for making and keeping promises to policyholders (promising to pay on death, disability, maturity, or retirement) then the Policy Administration System (PAS) is the machine’s engine. Every promise the insurer makes to every policyholder is recorded in the PAS. Every premium the policyholder pays flows through the PAS. Every claim is processed against the PAS record. Every reinsurance cession is calculated from PAS data. Every regulatory return is derived from PAS outputs. When the PAS works well, the insurer works well. When the PAS fails, corrupts data, cannot produce required reports, or cannot support a new product or distribution channel; the insurer’s entire operational capability is compromised.

Despite its centrality, the PAS is one of the most underinvested systems in many Nigerian life insurers. The industry historically grew through relationship-based distribution and manual processes, and many companies operate PAS platforms that are decades old, poorly documented, and incapable of supporting the regulatory demands of NIIRA 2025, the IFRS 17 reporting standard, the NDPA 2023 data governance requirements, and the digital channel expectations of a new generation of insurance buyers.

This chapter provides a comprehensive treatment of the PAS for Nigerian life insurance practitioners: what it is, what it must do, how to select and implement one, what it must produce, how it integrates with other systems, and how to evaluate whether the current PAS is fit for the demands of the post-NIIRA 2025 market.

blocks.text: 29.2 What Is a Policy Administration System?

blocks.h: The core software system that creates, stores, and manages all insurance policy records across the policy lifecycle, from application and underwriting through issuance, premium management, policy servicing, claims processing, and eventual termination (by lapse, surrender, maturity, or death). The PAS is the system of record for all policyholder obligations and the primary source of data for actuarial reserving, regulatory reporting, financial accounting, and management information.

The PAS sits at the centre of a life insurer’s technology ecosystem. It is not the only system the insurer operates (it interfaces with CRM platforms, actuarial systems, financial accounting systems, regulatory reporting tools, and digital customer channels) but it is the authoritative source of truth for the insurer’s policy portfolio. Any data about a policy that conflicts between the PAS and another system should be resolved in favour of the PAS record, unless the PAS record itself is demonstrably in error.
The distinction between the PAS and adjacent systems is critical to understand:

rows: PAS vs CRM (Customer Relationship Management)

The CRM manages the insurer’s relationships with prospects, agents, and policyholders, interactions, leads, activities, and communication history. The PAS manages the actual policy contracts, premium records, and obligation data. In a well-integrated technology stack, a sales agent’s CRM view of a policyholder’s profile draws real-time policy data from the PAS via API.
PAS vs Actuarial System

The actuarial system uses policy data extracted from the PAS (typically via a data extract or data warehouse) to perform reserving calculations, pricing model validation, and ORSA stress testing. The actuarial system’s outputs (reserve amounts, profit source analysis) feed back into the PAS’s financial reporting modules. The PAS holds the raw data; the actuarial system holds the analytical model.
PAS vs Financial Accounting System (ERP)

The financial accounting or ERP system records premium income, claims expenditure, commission payments, and investment transactions for financial reporting purposes. The PAS generates the source transactions (premium billings, claims settlements, commission calculations); the ERP records them as financial journal entries. In an integrated stack, PAS-generated transactions flow automatically into the ERP via API or batch interface.
PAS vs Digital Customer Portal

The digital customer portal (mobile app or web portal) is the customer’s interface, it allows policyholders to view their policy details, pay premiums, submit claims notifications, and update personal information. All of these actions read from or write to the PAS. The portal is the frontend; the PAS is the backend.
PAS vs Claims Management System

Some larger insurers operate a separate Claims Management System (CMS) that manages the claims workflow, notification, assessment, investigation, approval, and settlement. In most Nigerian life insurers, claims management functionality is embedded within the PAS itself rather than being a separate system.

blocks.h: A fully functional life insurance PAS comprises eight core modules, each managing a distinct stage of the policy lifecycle. Understanding each module’s functions, data inputs, and outputs is essential for both selecting and configuring a PAS, and for evaluating whether an existing PAS is meeting the insurer’s operational and regulatory requirements.

The new business module handles the journey from application submission to policy issuance. It captures all proposal form data (personal details, health declarations, benefit selections, beneficiary nominations), routes the application through the underwriting workflow, records the underwriting decision, generates the policy number, and creates the master policy record.

rows: Key functions

Application capture (manual data entry, digital form intake, API intake from digital channels); underwriting workflow routing (straight-through processing for clean risks, referral queue for complex risks); underwriting decision recording (acceptance, rating, exclusion, decline); policy number generation; policy document production; issuance notification to policyholder and agent.
Critical data captured

Policyholder identity (NIN, BVN, date of birth, address); life assured health data (medical history, current conditions, test results); benefit structure (product code, sum assured, premium, term, riders); agent / intermediary details; beneficiary nominations; premium payment method and bank account details.
NIIRA 2025 / regulatory link

All data captured at new business must be sufficient to support the insurer’s regulatory obligations: AML/KYC verification (NIN, BVN, identity documents); NDPA 2023 consent recording; premium basis alignment with NAICOM-approved product; commission calculation at the approved rate.
Quality control

NIGO (Not In Good Order) detection: the PAS should flag incomplete or inconsistent applications before they enter the underwriting queue, reducing the cycle time for applications that require re-work from the agent.

blocks.h: The policy issuance module generates the formal insurance contract and associated documentation for the policyholder. In a digital-first PAS, this includes automated generation of the policy document (PDF), the welcome letter, the premium payment instructions, and the direct debit mandate.

items.h: Policy document generation: The PAS populates the approved policy wording template (itself a NAICOM product-approved document) with the policyholder’s specific schedule data to produce a personalised policy document. The document generation must be triggered within the NIIRA 2025 product approval framework, only approved wordings may be issued.

Free look period tracking: The PAS must record the policy delivery date and calculate the free look period expiry date. Any cancellation request received within the free look period triggers an automatic premium refund and policy cancellation.
Certificate issuance for group life: For group life policies, the PAS generates individual member certificates for each eligible employee, summarising their specific coverage under the master policy.

blocks.h: Premium collection is the most operationally complex module in a life insurance PAS, because the consequences of premium management errors are severe: under-collected premiums create financial shortfalls; incorrectly lapsed policies create regulatory exposure (premature lapse without proper grace period management); and unreconciled premium receipts create ghost policies, records that show premiums paid but where the payment cannot be matched to a bank receipt.

rows: Premium billing generation

The PAS generates a premium billing schedule for each policy at inception, showing every premium due date and amount across the policy term. Premium reminders (SMS, email, WhatsApp) are triggered automatically by the PAS from this schedule.
Premium receipt recording

Each premium payment received (via direct debit, electronic transfer, mobile money, or cash through an agent) is matched to the policy’s premium schedule by the PAS reconciliation module. Matched receipts update the policy’s premium payment status; unmatched receipts enter a suspense account for manual investigation.
Grace period management

When a premium is not received on the due date, the PAS automatically enters the grace period (typically 30 days, as stated in the policy conditions). The policy remains in force during the grace period. If payment is received within the grace period, the policy is updated as current. If not, the PAS triggers the lapse workflow.
Lapse processing

On lapse, the PAS calculates the surrender value (if any), generates the lapse notification letter, removes the policy from the active in-force register, and triggers the conservation workflow (outreach to the policyholder by the customer service or agent team).
Premium reconciliation

The daily premium reconciliation process matches the PAS’s expected premium income against the insurer’s bank receipts. The reconciliation difference (unmatched debits or credits) must be investigated and cleared within a defined period. Unreconciled premium gaps are a significant audit finding and a potential indicator of premium theft.

blocks.h: The policy maintenance module handles all changes to an in-force policy after issuance: policyholder address changes, beneficiary nomination changes, premium frequency changes, sum assured alterations, rider additions or removals, policy loans, and reinstatements. Every change must be recorded with an audit trail that captures: who requested the change, who authorised it, when it was effective, and what the previous and new values were.

items.h: Endorsement processing: Material changes to policy terms are recorded as formal endorsements in the PAS. The endorsement record links to the policy record, creating a complete history of all changes made to the policy since inception.

Reinstatement workflow: The PAS manages the reinstatement application process: receiving the reinstatement request, calculating the outstanding premiums and interest due, routing the medical evidence for underwriting review (where required), recording the reinstatement decision, and updating the policy’s lapse status.

Policy loan management: Where the product permits policy loans, the PAS calculates the maximum loan available (based on the surrender value), records the loan disbursement, calculates monthly interest, reduces the available surrender value by the outstanding loan balance, and (if applicable) deducts the outstanding loan from any claim payment.

blocks.h: The benefit calculation module computes the value of benefits payable under each policy at any given point in the policy’s life: the current surrender value, the paid-up value (if premiums were stopped), the death benefit (including any accumulated bonuses for participating policies), and the maturity benefit. These calculations must align precisely with the product’s NAICOM-approved benefit structure and the actuarial assumptions certified by the Statutory Actuary.

For participating (with-profits) policies, the benefit calculation module must record the bonus declarations made each year and apply them to each individual policy. The bonus record must be auditable; the Statutory Actuary’s annual investigation will verify that declared bonuses have been correctly applied to all eligible policies.

The claims processing module manages the end-to-end claims workflow from notification to settlement. Under NIIRA 2025 (s.210) the insurer must settle valid claims within 60 days of notification; the book also recommends acknowledging claims within 5 business days as an internal service standard. The claims module must be designed to support these statutory timelines through automated workflow, escalation triggers, and SLA monitoring.

rows: Claims notification

Intake of the claim notification (via phone, email, in-branch, or digital portal). The PAS records the notification date, creates a claim reference number, and initiates the 5-day acknowledgement timer and the 60-day settlement timer.
Documentation management

Tracking of all required documents (death certificate, proof of identity, medical reports, employer records for group life). The PAS flags outstanding documents and sends automated reminders to the claimant.
Claims assessment workflow

Routing the claim to the appropriate assessor based on the claim type and amount. For claims above a defined threshold, the PAS routes to senior assessors and, for potential fraud, to the Special Investigation Unit (SIU). All assessment actions and decisions are recorded with timestamps.
Settlement calculation

Computing the benefit payable: the sum assured less any outstanding policy loan, plus any accumulated bonus (participating policies), less any outstanding premium (where death occurs during grace period). The calculation is driven by the benefit calculation module.
Payment processing
Generating the payment instruction and transmitting it to the insurer’s bank for electronic transfer to the claimant’s account. The PAS records the payment reference and the payment date.
NIIRA 2025 SLA monitoring

The claims module must generate a real-time dashboard showing the settlement status of all open claims against the 5-day and 60-day timelines. Claims approaching the deadline trigger escalation alerts to the Claims Manager and, if not resolved, to the COO. A claim that breaches the 60-day deadline triggers a regulatory breach notification workflow.

blocks.h: For insurers with reinsurance treaties (the majority of Nigerian life insurers), the PAS must calculate and record reinsurance cessions, the portion of each policy’s risk (and premium) transferred to reinsurers under the treaty. The reinsurance module reads the policy data, applies the treaty terms, computes the cession for each policy, aggregates cessions into treaty statements, and tracks reinsurance recoveries on claims.

items.h: Automatic treaty processing: The PAS applies the treaty’s cession formula (quota share percentage or surplus line calculation) to each eligible policy automatically at issuance. The treaty’s retention limit, reinsurer’s lines, and cession percentages are configured in the PAS’s reinsurance module.

Treaty statement generation: At the treaty accounting period (typically quarterly or annually), the PAS generates the reinsurance treaty statement (a detailed cession schedule listing every policy ceded, the ceded premium, the ceded reserve, and any recoveries on claims) for submission to the reinsurer and the reinsurance broker.

Domestic cession compliance (NIIRA 2025): The PAS must track the proportion of each treaty that is ceded to domestic reinsurers (Continental Re, NRC) versus international reinsurers, to demonstrate compliance with NIIRA 2025’s domestic cession requirement. The domestic cession report is a NAICOM statutory return requirement.

blocks.h: The financial reporting interface generates the data outputs that feed the insurer’s financial accounting system, actuarial reporting, and NAICOM regulatory returns. These outputs include: premium income recognised in the period; claims paid; commission paid; policy reserve movements; lapse income; reinsurance premium ceded; and the in-force policy count and aggregate sum assured (for the NAICOM quarterly return).

For IFRS 17 compliance, the financial reporting interface must produce the granular contract group data required for the IFRS 17 measurement models (the contractual service margin [CSM], the risk adjustment, and the liability for remaining coverage) at the level of policy cohorts defined by the insurer’s accounting policy. This is a significantly more complex data output than IFRS 4 required, and many legacy PAS platforms cannot produce it without extensive customisation or a middleware data transformation layer.

blocks.text: 29.4 Key Management Reports from a Life Insurance PAS

blocks.h: A well-configured PAS must produce a defined set of management and operational reports that enable the insurer’s management team to monitor business performance, identify emerging problems, and manage operational compliance. The following reports are the minimum expected from a functional life insurance PAS in the Nigerian market. Their absence, or their production only through manual extraction and manipulation, is a significant operational risk indicator.

blocks.text: 29.5 Cloud vs On-Premise PAS Deployment for Nigerian Insurers

blocks.h: The decision whether to deploy a PAS in the cloud (hosted on the infrastructure of a cloud service provider such as AWS, Azure, or a local Nigerian cloud provider) or on-premise (on servers hosted in the insurer’s own data centre) is one of the most consequential technology architecture decisions a Nigerian life insurer can make. It affects cost structure, scalability, data governance, security posture, and regulatory compliance.

rows: Dimension
Cloud Deployment
On-Premise Deployment
Capital cost
Low upfront investment. Typically subscription-based (pay per user or per policy). Eliminates the large initial server hardware investment.
High upfront investment in servers, storage, networking equipment, and data centre infrastructure. Depreciates over 5–7 years.
Operating cost
Predictable monthly subscription fee plus data egress costs. Scales up as policy count grows (cost advantage). Risk of cost escalation if usage patterns exceed contracted tiers.
Lower ongoing licence fees. Internal IT team cost. Risk of underutilisation (over-provisioned hardware capacity). Maintenance and upgrade costs are discrete capital events.
Scalability
Inherently scalable: cloud infrastructure can be scaled up during peak periods (year-end policy issuance, December claim surges) without hardware procurement.
Limited by the hardware capacity installed. Scaling requires hardware procurement lead time of weeks to months.
Data localisation (NDPA 2023 / GAID 2025)

Nigerian policyholder data must be stored on servers physically located in Nigeria (primary storage). Nigerian cloud providers (Galaxy Backbone, MainOne, 21st Century Technologies) can satisfy this requirement. International cloud providers (AWS Lagos, Azure South Africa) may satisfy the requirement depending on NDPC guidance.
By definition compliant: servers are in the insurer’s own data centre on Nigerian soil. No data localisation risk.
Cybersecurity

Cloud providers typically invest more in security infrastructure than individual insurers can afford. Shared responsibility model: the cloud provider secures the infrastructure; the insurer secures the application and data. Concentration risk: a cloud provider breach affects all customers.
Full control over physical security, access controls, and network architecture. Requires significant internal security investment and expertise to match enterprise cloud security standards.
Business continuity
Cloud providers typically offer built-in redundancy, failover, and disaster recovery across multiple data centres. RTO and RPO targets are contractually guaranteed.
Requires separate disaster recovery site, replication, and failover infrastructure, significant additional cost. RTO/RPO depends on the insurer’s own investment.
Vendor dependency
Dependent on cloud provider availability and pricing. Service disruption or contract termination by the cloud provider can be operationally catastrophic without a migration plan.
Complete control over infrastructure. No dependency on cloud provider availability. Hardware obsolescence risk if refresh cycle is not maintained.
NAICOM / regulatory posture

NAICOM’s Insurtech Guidelines (2025) acknowledge cloud deployment as a legitimate infrastructure model, subject to data localisation compliance and cybersecurity standards. NAICOM may require evidence of the cloud provider’s security certifications (ISO 27001, SOC 2).
No specific regulatory advantage over cloud. NAICOM’s inspection of on-premise infrastructure focuses on access controls, backup integrity, and disaster recovery capability.
Recommended for
Start-up and mid-size insurers; insurers implementing a new PAS; insurers prioritising flexibility and lower capital cost; Standalone Insurtechs.

Large established insurers with significant existing on-premise infrastructure investment; insurers with regulatory certainty requirements that cloud cannot currently satisfy; insurers in markets where reliable internet connectivity for cloud access cannot be guaranteed.

blocks.title: Advisory: Hybrid Deployment: The Pragmatic Nigerian Solution

blocks.h: Many Nigerian life insurers are adopting a hybrid deployment model: the core PAS runs on-premise (preserving data localisation certainty and the existing infrastructure investment), while new digital capabilities (the customer portal, the mobile app, the agent onboarding platform, and the analytics layer) run on cloud infrastructure. This ‘cloud-first for new, on-premise for core’ approach allows the insurer to modernise its customer-facing technology without committing to a full cloud migration of a complex legacy PAS. The risk is integration complexity: the on-premise PAS and cloud-based digital tools must exchange data reliably and securely.

A modern life insurance PAS does not operate in isolation. It is the hub of an integration network connecting multiple operational systems. The quality of these integrations (their reliability, real-time capability, data fidelity, and error handling) determines whether the insurer’s technology ecosystem functions as a coherent operational machine or as a collection of disconnected systems that require expensive manual reconciliation.

A defined protocol that enables two software systems to exchange data and trigger actions in real time over a network connection, without human intervention. In insurance, APIs enable a digital customer portal to query the PAS for a real-time policy status; a bancassurance bank system to trigger a new policy application in the PAS; or a claims management workflow tool to update the PAS’s claims status when a payment is authorised.

Legacy PAS platforms typically communicate through batch file exchanges, large data files exported from one system and imported into another at defined intervals (overnight, weekly). This approach produces stale data, reconciliation challenges, and an inability to support real-time digital customer experiences. A modern PAS must offer REST or SOAP API connectivity as a standard feature, enabling real-time data exchange with all integrated systems.

Data Exchanged

Nigerian Context
Core Banking System (Bancassurance)
New policy applications; premium collection mandates; policy status queries; claims payment instructions.
Bidirectional: bank to PAS (applications, premium receipts); PAS to bank (policy confirmations, claims payments).

Enables bancassurance channel operation: bank customers can apply for insurance through the bank’s internet banking or branch system, with the application flowing directly into the PAS’s new business queue.
CBN regulatory requirements on bank data sharing with insurance partners must be satisfied. The bancassurance agreement must specify the API integration standards and data protection obligations.
CRM Platform
Policyholder contact details; policy portfolio summary; service interaction history; renewal reminders.
PAS to CRM (policy data); CRM to PAS (policy updates initiated by service team).
Enables agent and customer service teams to see a 360° view of the policyholder’s insurance relationship without logging into the PAS directly.
Many Nigerian insurers use local CRM implementations or WhatsApp Business API as a CRM substitute. API integration must work with these lightweight tools as well as enterprise CRM platforms.
Actuarial / Valuation System
Policy data extract (product, age, benefit, premium, status) for reserve calculation; mortality experience data for assumption setting.
PAS to actuarial system (data extract, typically nightly or monthly); actuarial system to PAS (reserve amounts for financial reporting).
Enables the Statutory Actuary’s annual investigation and IFRS 17 measurement by providing clean, complete policy data in the format required by the actuarial model.

IFRS 17 requires policy-level data on cohort membership, inception date, and liability measurement group. Legacy PAS platforms often cannot produce this granularity without significant data transformation.
Financial Accounting / ERP System
Premium income transactions; claims payments; commission disbursements; reinsurance premium ceded; reserve movements.
PAS to ERP (financial transactions, daily or real-time); ERP to PAS (payment confirmations).

Enables automated financial reporting without manual re-keying of PAS financial data into the accounting system. Eliminates a significant source of financial reporting error and reconciliation effort.
SAP, Oracle, and Sage are common ERP platforms in Nigerian insurance. The PAS vendor must either provide a pre-built ERP connector or offer an open API for custom integration.
NAICOM Regulatory Reporting Portal
Quarterly market returns (new business count and premium, in-force register, claims settlement data, solvency margin, domestic cession ratio).
PAS to NAICOM portal (quarterly, via NAICOM’s mandated data format).
Enables compliance with NAICOM’s statutory reporting requirements without manual extraction and formatting of PAS data.
NAICOM’s digital filing portal requires data submission in a specific format (XML or structured CSV). The PAS must generate this output directly.
Digital Customer Portal / Mobile App
Policy details; premium payment history; premium due dates; claims status; policy documents.
Bidirectional: PAS to portal (read-only policy data); portal to PAS (premium payments, service requests, claims notifications).
Enables policyholders to self-serve: check their policy status, pay premiums, submit a claim notification, or download their policy document without contacting the insurer.
NDPA 2023 consent management: the portal must capture and record policyholder consent for data processing, with consent status stored in the PAS.
WhatsApp Business API / USSD
Premium reminders; payment confirmations; claims notifications; policy status queries.
PAS to WhatsApp/USSD (outbound notifications); WhatsApp/USSD to PAS (inbound queries, triggered by policyholder actions).

In the Nigerian market, WhatsApp and USSD are often more reliable and more widely used than mobile apps or email for policyholder communication. PAS integration with these channels is not optional; it is essential for effective policyholder engagement.
NAICOM’s USSD insurance distribution guidelines (Log 3A, 2020 Circular) require that USSD-distributed products are properly connected to a NAICOM-approved PAS backend.

blocks.text: 29.7 PAS Compliance: NIIRA 2025, NDPA 2023, and IFRS 17

rows: NIIRA 2025 Requirement
PAS Implication
Claims settlement: 5-day acknowledgement + 60-day settlement timeline

The PAS claims module must: timestamp the date and time of every claim notification; calculate the 60-day settlement deadline automatically; generate escalation alerts as the deadline approaches; and produce the NAICOM claims settlement report showing compliance status for every claim.
Premium receipt confirmation

The no-premium-no-cover principle requires the PAS to block policy activation until a confirmed premium receipt is matched to the new business record. No policy should be shown as ‘in-force’ in the PAS until premium receipt is confirmed.
Agent licensing compliance

The PAS’s agent module must hold each agent’s CIIN Cert. COP number and licence expiry date. The PAS should block commission payment to an agent whose licence has lapsed and should alert the Agency Manager to unlicensed agent production.
Commission compliance

Commission calculations in the PAS must be configured at the NAICOM-approved rates for each product. Commission payments above the approved rate are a regulatory breach; the PAS configuration is the primary control against this.
Audit trail for governance

NIIRA 2025’s three lines of defence framework requires the insurer to demonstrate that risk controls are operating. The PAS must maintain a complete, tamper-evident audit trail of every material action: policy issuance, premium receipt, policy change, claims decision, and commission payment, with user identity, timestamp, and the before/after values for every data change.

blocks.title: Data Protection Obligations Embedded in the PAS

blocks.h: The PAS is the primary system processing the personal data of Nigerian life insurance policyholders. Every NDPA 2023 obligation applies to how the PAS stores, accesses, and manages this data.

• Consent management: The PAS must record the specific consent given by each policyholder at application (for medical data processing, for marketing, for data sharing) and must flag any processing that goes beyond the recorded consent.
• Data subject access rights: The PAS must be able to generate a complete data extract for any policyholder who exercises their NDPA 2023 right of access, within 30 days of the request.

• Data minimisation: The PAS configuration must limit data capture to what is strictly necessary for the insurance contract. Data fields that are collected ‘just in case’ without a lawful basis violate the NDPA 2023’s data minimisation principle.

• Retention and disposal: The PAS must enforce the retention schedule: active policies (retained for the policy term plus 7 years); claims records (retained for 10 years). Records beyond their retention period must be automatically scheduled for deletion.

• Access control and data access logging: The PAS must enforce role-based access controls (no user can access data beyond what their role requires) and must log all access to policyholder health and financial data with user identity and timestamp.

blocks.text: 29.8 PAS Vendors in the African and Nigerian Market

blocks.h: The PAS market for African life insurers comprises four broad categories: global enterprise platforms adapted for the African market; regional African-developed platforms; Nigeria-specific local solutions; and bespoke internally developed systems. Each category has different cost profiles, capability ranges, and support models.

Oracle Insurance Policy Administration (OIPA); Majesco; EIS Suite; Sapiens; Guidewire.

Mid-size African insurers; regional groups operating across multiple African markets; insurers needing African market regulatory compliance built in.

Smaller vendor R&D budgets mean slower feature development; IFRS 17 capability may require additional modules; vendor viability risk for smaller providers.
Nigeria-Specific Solutions
Locally developed platforms by Nigerian software houses; customised versions of ERP systems (Sage, Tally) used as de facto PAS; hybrid spreadsheet-database systems.
Start-up insurers; very small insurers; companies with highly bespoke product structures that commercial PAS platforms cannot accommodate.
Fully customised for the Nigerian regulatory environment; lower initial cost; responsive local development team.
Limited scalability; high technical debt; poor audit trail capability; typically cannot produce IFRS 17-compliant data without major rework; vendor risk (dependency on a single developer).
Bespoke Internal Development
Internally developed platforms built by the insurer’s own IT team or a contracted development house.
Historically common among large Nigerian insurers with significant IT resources; now generally avoided for new builds.
Complete control over functionality; no licence fees; competitive advantage if done well.

Extremely high total cost of ownership when ongoing maintenance, upgrade, and regulatory change costs are included; knowledge concentration risk (if the internal developers leave, the system becomes unmaintainable); generally cannot match commercial platforms on IFRS 17, API capability, or security standards.

blocks.text: 29.9 PAS Selection Criteria for Nigerian Life Insurers

blocks.h: The selection of a PAS is one of the most consequential and irreversible technology decisions a life insurer can make. A poorly selected PAS will constrain the insurer’s operational capability, regulatory compliance, and digital ambition for a decade or more. The following criteria framework provides the basis for a structured PAS evaluation process.

rows: Criterion
What to Evaluate
Weight (Indicative)
Red Flag
Functional completeness

Does the platform support all eight core PAS modules? Does it handle the specific product types the insurer writes (participating policies, unit-linked, group life, annuities)? Can it be configured for new product structures without custom development?
High
A platform that requires significant custom development to support the insurer’s existing products is immediately problematic.
NIIRA 2025 regulatory compliance
Does the platform natively support: NAICOM reporting format; the claims SLA monitoring required by NIIRA 2025; agent licensing compliance checks; commission configuration at NAICOM-approved rates?
High (mandatory)
A PAS that cannot produce the NAICOM quarterly return in the correct format without manual extraction is non-compliant with regulatory obligations.
IFRS 17 readiness
Can the platform produce policy-level data in the format required for IFRS 17 CSM calculation? Does it maintain cohort assignment data from policy inception?
High (for listed insurers)
Many legacy platforms require a complete data transformation layer to produce IFRS 17-compliant outputs. This is a significant hidden cost.
NDPA 2023 compliance
Does the platform support: role-based access control; data access logging; consent management at the field level; data subject access request data extraction; retention and disposal enforcement?
High (mandatory)
A PAS with no data access logging capability is structurally non-compliant with NDPA 2023’s accountability obligations.
API capability

Does the platform offer REST APIs for real-time integration with CRM, digital portals, bancassurance banking systems, and USSD platforms? Is the API documentation publicly available and well-maintained?
High
A PAS without open API connectivity cannot support digital channel integration and will require expensive batch file workarounds.
Scalability
Can the platform handle the insurer’s projected 5-year policy count without performance degradation? Has the vendor demonstrated performance at scale in comparable markets?
Medium-High
A platform that has only been deployed at small insurer scale in similar markets is unproven.
Total cost of ownership (TCO)
What is the total 5-year cost: licence fees + implementation + customisation + training + ongoing support + upgrade costs? How does this compare to the value of operational improvements?
Medium
A very low headline licence fee that conceals high implementation and customisation costs is a common PAS procurement trap.
Vendor viability and support

How long has the vendor been operating? What is their financial position? Do they have an active development roadmap? What is the support model (24/7, local, remote)? What are the SLAs for issue resolution?
Medium-High
A PAS vendor with no other clients in Nigeria or the West African region will have no local market knowledge and no demonstrated ability to support the regulatory environment.
Data migration capability
How will historical policy data be migrated from the current system? Has the vendor done comparable migrations? What is the data validation and testing approach?
High (if replacing an existing system)
A vendor who cannot articulate a credible data migration methodology should not be selected for a PAS replacement project.
Cloud deployment option
Does the vendor offer a cloud deployment option with Nigerian data localisation capability (data centre in Nigeria)? What is the vendor’s cloud security certification?
Medium (depending on deployment preference)

blocks.text: 29.10 PAS Implementation: Governance, Risk, and Common Failure Modes

blocks.h: PAS implementation projects are among the most complex and highest-risk technology initiatives a life insurer can undertake. Policy data migration, regulatory continuity, agent tool disruption, and operational paralysis during the cutover are all genuine risks that have derailed PAS implementations in comparable markets. The following governance framework and failure mode inventory are based on Nigerian and African market implementation experience.

EXECUTIVE SPONSOR: The CEO or COO must own the PAS implementation at ExCo level. A PAS implementation that is managed purely at IT level will fail, the cross-functional decisions required (data migration priorities, product configuration, regulatory reporting requirements, agent tool design) cannot be made without executive authority and cross-departmental coordination.

STEERING COMMITTEE: A steering committee comprising the CEO/COO, CFO, Head of Operations, Head of IT, Chief Distribution Officer, and the Statutory Actuary must meet at least fortnightly during implementation. The steering committee resolves escalated issues that the project team cannot resolve within the implementation timeline.

PROJECT MANAGEMENT: An experienced implementation project manager (who has delivered at least one life insurance PAS implementation) must lead the project. The insurer’s project manager works alongside the vendor’s implementation team. Project milestones, risk register, and issue log must be reviewed at every steering committee meeting.

DATA MIGRATION: The data migration from the old PAS to the new PAS is the highest-risk element of the implementation. All historical policy data must be: extracted from the old system; cleansed and standardised; validated against the old system’s reports; migrated to the new system; and re-validated against the new system’s reports. No cutover should proceed until the data migration validation confirms that the new system’s in-force register matches the old system’s register exactly.

USER ACCEPTANCE TESTING (UAT): A structured UAT programme must test every material business scenario before go-live: policy issuance across all product types; premium collection and lapse processing; claims processing and settlement; reinsurance cession calculation; all management reports against expected values; all regulatory report outputs. UAT must be conducted by business users, not IT staff. Sign-off authority for UAT completion rests with the COO and the Statutory Actuary.

blocks.title: Common PAS Implementation Failure Modes in the Nigerian Market

blocks.h: 1. DIRTY DATA MIGRATION: The most common failure mode. Policy data accumulated over years in a legacy system is frequently inconsistent, incomplete, and inaccurate. Migrating dirty data into a new PAS simply perpetuates the data quality problems in a more expensive system. A data cleansing project must precede migration.

2. UNDERESTIMATING CONFIGURATION COMPLEXITY: Commercial PAS platforms are highly configurable but require significant configuration effort to match a specific insurer’s product structures, commission rules, and regulatory reporting requirements. Insurers that underestimate this effort (and the internal resource required to manage it) consistently overshoot implementation timelines and budgets.

3. PARALLEL RUN SKIPPED: The parallel run (operating both the old and new PAS simultaneously for a defined period [typically 1–3 months], comparing their outputs daily) is the most effective risk mitigation for a PAS go-live. Under pressure to meet a go-live deadline, many implementations skip the parallel run and go directly to cutover. This is the decision most regretted when issues emerge.

4. INADEQUATE CHANGE MANAGEMENT: A new PAS changes the daily working tools of every member of the operations, sales support, claims, and finance teams. Inadequate training, insufficient user involvement in the UAT process, and poor communication about what is changing and when produces a workforce that is demotivated, resistant, and prone to error at go-live.

5. NO REGULATORY CONTINUITY PLAN: The NAICOM quarterly return does not pause for a PAS implementation. The NIIRA 2025 claims settlement timelines do not pause. A PAS implementation that does not include a regulatory continuity plan (ensuring all regulatory obligations continue to be met during the transition period) will generate NAICOM findings for late or incorrect submissions.

Most Nigerian life insurers currently operate a PAS that was implemented more than ten years ago, against a regulatory and technology environment that is radically different from today’s. The question is not whether the current PAS needs to change (for most Nigerian insurers, it does) but how urgently, and through what route.

blocks.title: Advisory: A PAS Assessment Framework for Nigerian Life Insurers

blocks.h: STEP 1: REGULATORY COMPLIANCE AUDIT. Can the current PAS produce every NAICOM statutory return in the correct format, without manual extraction and manipulation? Can it enforce the NIIRA 2025 claims settlement SLAs? Can it produce the NDPA 2023 data access log? If the answer to any of these is NO, the insurer has an immediate regulatory compliance gap that must be closed.

STEP 2: MANAGEMENT INFORMATION QUALITY AUDIT. Can the current PAS produce all eight reports listed in Section 29.4 automatically, in a format that management can use directly without re-processing in Excel? Significant manual extraction and manipulation is a symptom of a PAS that the insurer has outgrown.

STEP 3: INTEGRATION CAPABILITY AUDIT. Does the current PAS have API connectivity to the insurer’s digital customer portal, bancassurance banking systems, and WhatsApp/USSD customer communication channels? An inability to integrate with digital channels through real-time APIs limits the insurer’s ability to compete with Insurtech entrants.

STEP 4: VENDOR VIABILITY AUDIT. Is the current PAS vendor actively investing in the platform? Is the platform being upgraded to meet IFRS 17, NDPA 2023, and NIIRA 2025 requirements? Is there an active user community? A PAS whose vendor has stopped active development is on a path to obsolescence.

STEP 5: TOTAL COST OF INACTION. The cost of upgrading or replacing a PAS is significant and visible. The cost of not upgrading (manual workarounds, regulatory findings, the inability to launch new products or distribution channels, IFRS 17 non-compliance) is diffuse and accumulates invisibly until a crisis makes it undeniable. Calculate both before deciding.

blocks.title: The Most Important PAS Investment Decision for a Nigerian Life Insurer

blocks.h: Invest in a PAS that will not require replacement again within five years. The temptation to choose a lower-cost, partial solution (a system that addresses the immediate regulatory compliance gap but cannot grow with the insurer’s digital ambitions) is a false economy. A well-chosen, well-implemented modern PAS with open API architecture, IFRS 17-native reporting, and NDPA 2023-compliant data governance is a one-generation investment that unlocks the insurer’s ability to compete in the digital insurance market. A cheap PAS that requires replacement in three years will cost more in total than the right PAS implemented once.

The core software system that creates, stores, and manages all insurance policy records across the policy lifecycle, from application through to termination. The system of record for all policyholder obligations.

The PAS module that handles the journey from application intake through underwriting to policy issuance, capturing all proposal form data and routing the application through the underwriting workflow.
The PAS module managing premium billing generation, premium receipt recording, grace period tracking, lapse processing, and premium reconciliation.
The PAS module handling all changes to an in-force policy after issuance, including endorsements, reinstatements, policy loans, and beneficiary changes, with complete audit trail.
The PAS module computing policy values: surrender value, paid-up value, death benefit (including bonuses for participating policies), and maturity benefit.

The PAS module managing the end-to-end claims workflow from notification to settlement, with automated SLA monitoring against the 60-day statutory settlement requirement (NIIRA 2025 s.210) and the insurer’s 5-day acknowledgement standard.
The PAS module calculating and recording reinsurance cessions under treaty arrangements, generating treaty statements, and tracking reinsurance recoveries on claims.
The PAS component generating data outputs for the financial accounting system, actuarial reporting, and NAICOM regulatory returns.
A complete list of all active policies with their key data; the definitive record of the insurer’s current policyholder obligations and the basis for actuarial reserving and NAICOM reporting.
The daily process of matching expected premium income (from the PAS billing schedule) against actual bank receipts, with investigation of unmatched items.

A defined protocol enabling two software systems to exchange data and trigger actions in real time; the modern standard for PAS integration with CRM, digital portals, banking systems, and regulatory reporting tools.
The NDPA 2023 / GAID 2025 requirement that personal data of Nigerian data subjects be stored primarily on servers physically located in Nigeria; material to cloud deployment decisions.
A structured testing programme conducted by business users (not IT staff) to verify that every material business scenario works correctly in the new PAS before go-live.

The practice of operating both the old and new PAS simultaneously for a defined period after go-live, comparing daily outputs to identify and resolve discrepancies before decommissioning the old system.
The full five-year cost of a PAS, including licence fees, implementation, customisation, training, support, and upgrade costs; the correct basis for PAS financial evaluation.
An application flagged by the PAS as incomplete or inconsistent, returned to the agent for correction before entering the underwriting queue.
